config.title: Validate Binary Search Tree

intro.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a function that checks whether a binary tree is a valid Binary Search Tree (BST). You'll learn the core concept of BST validation using recursion to traverse the tree while tracking valid value ranges for each node. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, recursion, and tree data structures. You'll implement a solution that efficiently validates the BST property by comparing node values with their allowed minimum and maximum bounds. This exercise will help you understand both tree traversal techniques and the specific constraints that define a proper BST.
intro.usecase: Validating binary search trees is crucial in systems that rely on hierarchical data organization, such as e-commerce product catalogs where categories and subcategories must maintain proper ordering for efficient searching. Database indexing engines use BST validation to ensure query performance remains optimal by keeping search trees properly structured. In file systems and directory structures, validation ensures that hierarchical data maintains the correct parent-child relationships for fast navigation and retrieval. This pattern also appears in gaming leaderboards and scoring systems where ranked data needs to maintain sorted order for quick updates and lookups.

objectives: Implement a recursive depth-first traversal to inspect all nodes in a binary tree
Apply the binary search tree property rules to validate node relationships
Construct a validation function that tracks minimum and maximum bounds for each subtree
Initialize and update boundary variables correctly during recursive traversal
Manipulate tree node values to test edge cases in the validation algorithm
Integrate boundary checking logic with tree traversal to validate the entire structure
Control the recursion flow to handle empty nodes and single-node trees

content.body: Imagine you're checking if a family tree follows a specific rule: parents must come before children in a certain order. In binary search trees, every node must be greater than its left branch and less than its right branch. Let's learn how to validate this efficiently.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
• Apply the BST property rules to validate a tree
• Implement a depth-first traversal to check each node
• Explain why we need to track valid value ranges as we explore branches
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Look at this small tree: root value 10, left child 5, right child 15. Does it follow the BST rule? (Left must be < parent, right must be > parent)
content.title: Try it

content.body: Now add a left child to node 5 with value 7. Is this still valid? Remember: all values in the left branch must be less than 10, and each node's own children must follow the same rule.
content.title: Explore deeper

content.body: What if node 5 had a right child with value 12? This value is greater than 5 (good) but also greater than 10 (bad for the left branch). Can you spot why this breaks the BST rule?
content.title: Find the violation

content.body: You manually checked each node against its parent and considered the whole branch. This is like exploring from the root down each branch, verifying rules at every step.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When trees have hundreds of nodes, manually checking becomes impossible. We need a systematic way to explore branches while remembering the valid value ranges for each part of the tree.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Think of exploring a tree like following paths from the root. As you go left, values must stay below a certain ceiling. As you go right, values must stay above a certain floor. We'll visit nodes one branch at a time, carrying these boundaries with us.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Show exploring from the root down branches; one level or one branch at a time.

content.body: We'll do a depth-first traversal, starting at the root with no boundaries. At each node, we check if its value fits within the current allowed range. Then we explore left with a new upper bound, and right with a new lower bound.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Start at root with range (-∞, +∞)
2. Check if current node's value is within current range
3. If not, tree is invalid
4. Recursively check left child with updated upper bound
5. Recursively check right child with updated lower bound
6. If we reach an empty node (null), that's valid (base case)
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the validation function
steps.instruction: Start by defining the main function that takes a tree root. We'll use a helper function for the recursive traversal.
steps.hint: The function should return a boolean.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the main validation function.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're defining a function that takes a root parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's start with the basic function structure: function isValidBST(root) {}

steps.title: Define the recursive helper
steps.instruction: Inside isValidBST, define a helper function that takes a node and lower/upper bounds. This will do the actual validation.
steps.hint: The helper needs node, low, and high parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure the helper takes three parameters: node, low, and high.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: we need a helper that can track boundaries as we traverse.

steps.title: Handle the base case
steps.instruction: In the validate helper, first handle the empty tree case. If node is null, return true.
steps.hint: Check if node is null or undefined.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! An empty tree or branch is always valid.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Make sure you're checking for null and returning true.
steps.feedbackWrong: The base case: when we reach the end of a branch (null), that path is valid.

steps.title: Check current node's value
steps.instruction: After the base case, check if the current node's value is within the allowed range. If not, return false.
steps.hint: The value must be greater than low and less than high.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! This ensures each node respects its boundaries.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Check both conditions: value must be > low AND < high.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: BST rule means node.val must be strictly between low and high.

steps.title: Recursively validate branches
steps.instruction: Finally, recursively validate the left and right branches with updated bounds. Return true only if both are valid.
steps.hint: Left branch gets current value as new high, right branch gets it as new low.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Make sure you're updating bounds correctly for left and right.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: left branch must be < current value, right branch must be > current value.

content.body: Great work! You've learned to validate a BST by exploring branches from the root, carrying value boundaries as you go. Remember: each node must be within its allowed range, and empty nodes are always valid. This depth-first approach efficiently checks the entire tree in O(n) time.
content.title: Done
